_about: Villes et tribus tunisiennes 1881, the sketch map in Andre Martel, Les Confins saharo-tripolitains de la Tunisie (1881-1911), Paris, P.U.F., 1965. Scale printed as 1/3.000.000 env. Every tribe name on it, read by eye, with the pixel it sits at.
_what_this_is_not: Not a sheet in this collection. The Gallica corpus this repository inventories holds no map of Martel's; this is a figure from a 1965 monograph, a historian's synthesis of where tribes were in 1881 drawn from French military and archival material. It is a secondary source and is kept in its own file, its own CSV and its own colour so that it is never pooled with the two primary sheets without the reader seeing it happen.
_why_it_is_here: It is the only whole-country tribal map in hand. The two transcribed sheets leave the south blank - the 1853 one was read only to about 34 N and the 1881 one gives everything below Sfax to a single tribe - and that blank was the largest hole in the figure. Martel names the Nefzaoua, the Djerid and the Dahar, so the blank can be tested rather than assumed.
_how_read: Read from a screen reproduction supplied in conversation, at roughly 1200 px across the sheet, in one pass. That is a coarser reading than the two Gallica sheets, which were read at full IIIF resolution over twenty tiles. Positions are the centre of the printed name; names set along an arc or broken around a line are anchored at their midpoint, as on the other sheets.
_projection_check: The fitted scales come out at 257 px per degree of longitude against 315 per degree of latitude, a ratio of 0.818 where cos(35 N) is 0.819. The sheet is plain equirectangular, which is what an affine assumes, so the fit below is the right model and its residual is reading error rather than projection error.
citation: Andre Martel, Les Confins saharo-tripolitains de la Tunisie (1881-1911), Paris, Presses universitaires de France, 1965. Map: 'Villes et tribus tunisiennes 1881'.
